Currently the way to pass a noise map to aer-executor is something like

```python
pm = generate_boxing_passmanager(tags="tag1", inject_noise=True)

samplex_arguments = {"inject_noise_ref1": some_noise_model}
map = {"tag1": another_noise_model}

executor = AerExecutor(backend=AerSimulator(), map)
job = executor.run(program)
```

There was a discussion on why `map` here is specified in `AerExecutor` constructor, when this `map` likely has a strong coupling to the input quantum program. The motivation was to avoid having to change the `run()` method invocation when switching between a simulator and a real QPU. 

This syntax might become a bit of problem when we want to add local mode support for Executor (#3055), which would allow

```python
backend = AerSimulator()
# backend = service.backend("ibm_torino")    # uncomment for real QPU

executor = Executor(backend)
job = executor.run(program)
```

To simplify the future local mode support, I suggest we instead add a `SimulatorOption` option class to Executor. These options are ignored if the backend is not a simulator. This allows one to do

```python
pm = generate_boxing_passmanager(tags="tag1", inject_noise=True)

samplex_arguments = {"inject_noise_ref1": some_noise_model}

# executor = Executor(backend)   # replace next line with this for real QPU
executor = AerExecutor(backend=AerSimulator())
executor.options.simulator.noise_map = {"tag1": another_noise_model}   # ignored if using real QPU
executor.options.simulator.seed_simulator = 123   # ignored if using real QPU

job = executor.run(program)
```

Note that 
1. The example above also has a `seed_simulator` option. Specifying a seed is very common. While that's an argument you can pass to `AerSimulator()`, it's not something you can pass to a fake backend constructor. Although alternatively this can be done using `backend=AerSimulator.from_backend(FakeTorino(), seed_simulator=123)`
2. There is an existing [SimulatorOptions](https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-ibm-runtime/blob/020b3cbdabaaee50dcb6aa816dfa512d1f1a0ae9/qiskit_ibm_runtime/options_models/simulator.py#L37) class. It was originally created for cloud simulators, and all of the options can already be pass directly to `AerSimulator()`

During a recent meeting with the addons team, it was brought up that we should monitor the RTT (round-trip time) of executor-based estimator (and sampler) jobs, to make sure that we don't take a hit on performance in the future without detecting it. 

RTT is defined as the time between pressing ENTER on `estimator.run(pubs)` to the time that I get `job.result()` back, minus the time spent in the queue and the "quantum" time spent running quantum circuits on the QPU. All these info is available somewhere, likely around the job metrics

I would be curious to know if we can augment the scope of the integration tests to also track RTT, for the reason that:
- Calculating RTT should be pretty straightforward, based on the info above
- We are already submitting jobs, may as well take full advantage of them

Monitoring (i.e., the act of comparing RTT with RTT of previous jobs) seems trickier though, and likely what needs investigation.

> This is a tricky PR to review

It is, thanks for the review!

> as it requires one to refresh one's memory about an object, QiskitRuntimeService, that hasn't been touched in a while.

I challenge / rephrase this a bit as:
* the `registries.py` file (in particular the callbacks) do require _some_ insight into `QiskitRuntimeService`, and more insight into the API responses. For the latter, I tried to solve via documentation. For the former, I could not find a way to avoid it.
* when tests are rewritten to use the decorator, they actually use the real `QiskitRuntimeService`. This makes it easier to refresh our memory of it - and actually, allows us to exercise the real implementation properly and rebuild that knowledge backed by reproducible tests. Previously, we could only use `FakeRuntimeService` (and `FakeRuntimeClient`, etc), which override methods and mock (python-land) items, so we could not really exercise `QiskitRuntimeService` in unit tests.

> It also adds a lot of lines of code in the registries.py file, which aren't super simple to grasp. However, I don't see them as adding maintenance burden

It does, and I actually see more a risk of a maintenance burden (it does have some boilerplate, the real complexity is in the callbacks and how they relate to `Backend` and `Instance`). The goal is to be selective on adding new features to the registry, and decide as needed (and not be shy on just opting not to cover some functionality). This will be better seen as we explore moving other files to the decorator.

Continuing but not as a options validator since it causes mutation order side effects. 

For example this is the behavior from the legacy that should not be reproduced:

```
# this works
legacy = LegacyEstimator(mode=backend)
legacy.options.resilience.zne_mitigation = True
legacy.options.resilience.zne.noise_factors = [1, 3, 4, 5]
legacy.options.resilience.zne.extrapolator = "double_exponential" 

# this doesnt
legacy = LegacyEstimator(mode=backend)
legacy.options.resilience.zne_mitigation = True
legacy.options.resilience.zne.extrapolator = "double_exponential" 
legacy.options.resilience.zne.noise_factors = [1, 3, 4, 5]
```

The solution is to put the validation later in the workflow.

Part of the discussion should be how much the simulators should align with results returned from real devices. My opinion is that it's ok to diverge: devices return a lot of information about chunking, scheduling, and stretches, while simulators return information about time taken, memory consumption, and parallelization. But I agree that we should take a closer look at what's done as part of #3406, and decide individually for each change whether to apply it also for the simulator.
